bio.en: Keith Yandell is a longtime DoorDash leader who has run the company's legal, HR, customer support, marketing, and corporate development teams, and previously led litigation at Uber.
bio.zh: 基思·扬德尔（Keith Yandell）是 DoorDash 的资深领导者，曾执掌公司的法务、人力资源、客户支持、市场营销以及企业发展团队，此前在 Uber 负责诉讼业务。

summary.en: Keith describes how a founder's drive is the single most decisive factor in a startup's survival through repeated rejection. He explains DoorDash's "no politics, no asshole" culture and the WeDash program that builds empathy by having employees deliver food. The episode offers a master class in leading diverse functions with empathy and giving people honest, growth-oriented feedback.
summary.zh: 基思指出，创始人的那股冲劲，是初创公司在一次次被拒绝后依然存活的最决定性因素。他阐释了 DoorDash"无政治、无混蛋"的文化，以及通过让员工亲自送餐来建立同理心的 WeDash 项目。本期是关于如何以同理心领导多元职能、并给予人们诚实且利于成长的反馈的大师课。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: Every business that you have heard of has gotten rejected by at least a handful of venture capitalists at one point or another. And so that drive to keep going if you believe in the business is critical, absolutely critical. I mean, we were weeks of runway situation and had been told no by everyone. And it was just Tony's drive, really, to keep going. And the way he explains it to me is it's just the difference between a founder and a non-founder. If you're really a founder, you just have to find a way. You have to keep going. There's no question. And I mean, that's the only advice I can give folks, is it only takes one yes. But you got to keep going.
turns.zh: 你们听说过的每一家企业，都曾在某个阶段被至少几位风险投资家拒绝过。所以，如果你对自己的业务深信不疑，那么坚持下去的动力至关重要，绝对至关重要。我记得我们当时资金链即将断裂，每个人都拒绝了我们。真正支撑我们走下去的，是托尼的坚韧。他是这么跟我解释的：这就是创始人和非创始人的区别。如果你真是一名创始人，就必须想办法克服困难，坚持下去。这毫无疑问。我能给出的唯一建议就是：只需要一个肯定的答复。但你必须不断前进。

turns.zh: 非常感谢邀请，Lenny。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: First off the bat, I just want to give a big thank you to Gokul Rajaram and Micah Moreau for suggesting you be on the podcast, helping make this happen, and also just suggesting a bunch of questions to ask you. So, I hope you're ready to be in the hot seat.
turns.zh: 首先，我要衷心感谢Gokul Rajaram和Micah Moreau向我推荐参加播客，协助促成这次访谈，还提出了许多值得探讨的问题。所以，我希望你能做好准备，迎接接下来的挑战。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: Definitely as ready as I'm going to be. And those are two good folks to talk to.
turns.zh: 我已经尽可能做好准备了。他们都是很棒的对话者。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. And Gokul's been on the podcast. Maybe we'll get Micah on the podcast at some point. I wanted to start off with a story. Apparently, there's a story of you interviewing what is now your VP of engineering. And I hear that in the interview, you called him an asshole. And more interestingly, he joined DoorDash because you did that. Can you just talk about that story and share that story?
turns.zh: 太棒了。Gokul已经上过播客了。或许我们日后也能邀请Micah参加。我想先讲个故事。显然，有个关于你面试现任工程副总裁的趣闻。据说在面试中，你称他是个混蛋。更有趣的是，他之所以加入DoorDash，就是因为你这么评价他。你能谈谈这个故事吗？

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: Yeah, actually, it wasn't during the interview. We were debriefing. And for me, one of the top things I always hear about DoorDash from an executive standpoint when we do the internal survey is it's a "no politics, no asshole" culture. And I'm not one to swear a lot, but after interviewing Ryan Sokol, who's now our VP of eng, he was just kind of aloof. He came off as aloof to me, really curt answers. And I just didn't have a great feeling about him. And I pride myself on being able to discern when people are really engaged or not. And I went to Tony Xu, who's our founder and CEO. I said, "Tony, I think this guy's a jerk. I don't think we want him at the company." And Tony was great. He said, "Keith, I want you to just have dinner with him, please, because I got a completely different impression. And if you have dinner with him, and you still think he's a jerk, we won't hire."
turns.zh: 嗯，实际上这不是在面试中发生的。那是在复盘环节。内部调查时，高管层常被问及DoorDash的企业文化是什么——“无政治、无混蛋”。我平时不太喜欢爆粗口，但面试现任工程副总裁Ryan Sokol时，他态度冷淡，回答简短，让我对他印象不佳。我自诩能判断对方是否真心投入。于是我去找创始人兼CEO Tony Xu，说：“Tony，我觉得这人挺混蛋的，我们公司不需要他。”Tony很通情达理：“Keith，你去和他共进晚餐吧，我另有判断。如果你还是觉得他混蛋，我们就不录用。”

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: And so I ended up meeting Ryan down the street. We actually live in the same general area. We went out to dinner, and I started right away. I said, "Ryan, during the interview you kind of seemed like an asshole. Are you an asshole?" And he was so great. It completely changed my perspective in a good two minutes. He wanted to know what he had said. He said, "I'm super embarrassed, and what could I do differently? Regardless of how this works out for me in this circumstance, that's just not how I want to be perceived." And we talked and joked about the things he had done, and he kind of told me the background for how he reacted or why he reacted the way he did. And by the end of the dinner, we ended up staying super late. We had a couple beers afterwards. Ryan and I have become really good friends.
turns.zh: 于是我们在街边见了面，住得挺近的。我们共进晚餐，我一开口就问：“Ryan，面试时你表现得像个混蛋。你就是个混蛋吗？”他反应超好。在两分钟内彻底改变了我的看法。他追问自己说了什么：“我很尴尬，有什么能改进的？无论结果如何，我都不想被这样看待。”我们聊笑起来，他还分享了自己的背景。晚餐结束时，我们聊到很晚，后来还喝了几杯啤酒，现在成了好朋友。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: And six months later, he told me that one of the reasons why he joined DoorDash was that we were going to blackball him potentially from joining just because of his attitude, because his perspective is life's too short to work with people you don't really enjoy, and a lot of people pay lip service. And he knew he was going to be a tough hire for us at the time. And the fact we were willing to go all the way down the path and have someone super qualified but didn't meet the culture bar, for him was what pushed him over the edge to join the company.
turns.zh: 六个月后，他告诉我，当时他加入DoorDash的动机之一，就是我们可能因为他的态度将他拒之门外。他的理念是人生短暂，不愿与不合拍的人共事，而多数人只是口头说说。他知道自己当时很难被录用，但我们愿意坚持标准，不达文化要求绝不录用，这最终打动了他加入。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. I love the directness of that meeting, of just like, "Are you an asshole?"
turns.zh: 我很欣赏这种直截了当的沟通方式，直接问“你是混蛋吗？”

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: Think about it, right? And if someone really was a jerk, they probably wouldn't have taken it very well. Right? It's just like when you're interviewing someone, giving them tough feedback after the interview if there's an area of concern, but you otherwise like them, can be a really great way to see how they would interact with you personally as well as how they take feedback. And so that was my learning from the situation, is if you really enjoy an interview, except for maybe something on the culture side, to give the direct feedback and see how people engage.
turns.zh: 想想看，对吧？如果有人真的很讨人厌，他们很可能无法接受这样的批评。是吧？就像你在面试别人时一样，如果面试后给出负面反馈，指出对方存在的问题，但你其实挺喜欢这个人的，这能很好地观察他们如何与你个人互动，以及他们如何接受反馈。这就是我从这次经历中得到的启发——如果你真的很享受面试过程，除了文化方面可能有些担忧之外，不妨直接给出反馈，看看对方的反应。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This touches on another question I wanted to ask you, which is just about DoorDash's culture, which feels really unique, just feels very driven, very pragmatic. There's a story I heard where when you guys celebrated one of your biggest milestones, you bought the cheapest champagne and plastic flutes, and I think the founders brought that to everyone. Could you just talk about what makes DoorDash's culture so interesting and unique? And maybe if there's a story of just a microcosm of what DoorDash culture is like, that'd be awesome to hear.
turns.zh: 这让我想起另一个我想问你的问题，那就是DoorDash的企业文化。它给人的感觉非常独特，充满了进取精神和务实态度。我听说有个故事，当你们庆祝公司重大里程碑时，买了最便宜的香槟和塑料杯，我想创始人还把这些杯子分发给大家。你能否谈谈DoorDash的文化为何如此有趣和独特？或许能分享一个能体现DoorDash文化微观面的故事，那就太棒了。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: Founder-led companies tend to take on the personality of their founders. And if you spend any time with our founder, Tony Xu, you realize that he's a humble leader. He's competitive. He really wants to win, and he'll do whatever it takes to win. And the example you're referring to, I think, is when we raised our Series D funding, which was a really tough fundraise for us... We had very little runway left. We almost went out of business, and it was a huge relief when we had finally gotten the funding secured.
turns.zh: 创始人主导的公司往往会带有创始人的个人风格。如果你和我们的创始人徐涛相处过，就会发现他是一位谦逊的领导者。他很有竞争意识，非常渴望胜利，会不惜一切代价去争取胜利。至于你提到的那个故事，我想应该是在我们筹集D轮融资的时候，那次融资对我们来说确实很艰难……当时我们几乎没有运营资金了，差点倒闭。最终成功融资后，大家如释重负。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: And I remember I was in a meeting. I was running policy and communications, among other things, at the time, and I was in the meeting with a couple other folks, and we were talking about the press release strategy. Tony was there. And someone ran down and got some, I think it was Korbel or something champagne and some plastic flutes. And one of the women who was in the meeting with me was going to leave to go put those together. This is a very smart woman, who I think Tony recognized could add more value. And he said, "Whoa, whoa, whoa. You stay here. I'm going to go put together the champagne flutes." And he called the other two co-founders, Andy Fang and Stanley Tang. They came, stayed up all night, put together... I don't know... 500 champagne flutes, plastic ones, for this cheap champagne and let the people who are closest to the problem try to work out the comms piece. And I do think that's one great example of the culture.
turns.zh: 我记得当时我在开会。我当时负责政策和沟通等工作，会议上还有其他几个人。我们在讨论新闻稿策略，托尼也在场。有人跑去拿了些香槟杯，可能是科贝尔之类的，还有塑料杯。和我一起开会的一位女士正要去整理这些杯子。这位女士非常聪明，我想托尼意识到她能为团队带来更多价值。于是他说：“等等，等等，等等。你留在这里。我去整理香槟杯。”他还叫来了另外两位联合创始人方安迪和唐斯坦利。他们通宵达旦地整理了……我不知道……500个塑料香槟杯，为这种廉价香槟配上杯子，让最贴近问题的人来研究沟通策略。我确实认为这就是文化的一个很好的例子。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: The other thing I think that really exemplifies DoorDash's culture is a level of customer obsession. And that manifests in a few different ways. We have a program called WeDash, where, four times, a year all employees are required to go do deliveries. And I love doing it. I do it more than four times a year, and I usually take my daughters with me. And one time, I was out with my daughter, who was eight at the time. We got a delivery, and it was not the best delivery. There's clearly something wrong with the system. We got a sandwich and a coffee, and we're supposed to drive 18 and a half miles to drop it off. And that didn't make sense for the customer. It didn't make sense for us as drivers.
turns.zh: 我认为DoorDash文化的另一个典型体现是客户至上。这体现在几个方面。我们有一个叫WeDash的项目，每年有四次全体员工必须去送餐。我很喜欢参与这个项目。我每年参与次数超过四次，还经常带上我的女儿们。有一次，我和当时八岁的女儿一起外出送餐。送的订单质量不佳。很明显系统出了问题。我们拿到了一个三明治和一杯咖啡，却被要求开车18.5英里去送货。这对客户来说毫无意义，对我们这些送餐员来说同样毫无意义。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: And she'd gotten to know Tony over the years, and she said, "I really want to call Tony and tell him this thing's broken." "Honey, I like my job. I'd like to keep my job. Can we not call Tony right now?" But she was adamant, and I was so proud of her for feeling so strongly that she wanted to fix this thing that was broken. I figured, "He's not going to answer anyway. We can just call." So call. Tony picks up on the first ring. And I'm like, "Oh, this might go badly." And she just lays into him. She said, "This is going to take us 36 minutes to drop off. The coffee's not going to be hot. How could you allow this experience if you really care about your customers?"
turns.zh: 这些年来，她逐渐了解了托尼。她说：“我真的想打电话告诉托尼这东西坏了。”“亲爱的，我喜欢我的工作。为了保住工作，我们还是别现在打给他吧？”但她态度坚决，我为她如此执着于修复损坏的东西感到骄傲。我心想：“反正他也不会接电话的，就打吧。”结果托尼第一声就接了。我心里一惊，心想：“这回可能要糟了。” 她直接开口：“我们要花 36 分钟去送货，咖啡肯定凉了。如果你们真心在乎客户体验，怎么能让这种情况发生？”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Whoa.
turns.zh: 哇哦。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: And I kind of sucked in my breath and said, "Well, that's how my time at DoorDash ended." But Tony was great. He was like, "Hey, Alice, we have people who do deliveries for months. We have people who deliveries for years, and they're always providing me feedback. And this is one of the most insightful pieces of feedback I've gotten recently. And you've only been dashing for a few different times." And by the time we got home, he'd actually sent an email out to the product organization, calling out the problem, suggesting the fix. And they were already working on it. And that shows the bias to action that I think really is at the heart of DoorDash, alongside that customer obsession. And it's not unusual for Tony to do customer support. It wasn't like just because he heard this from my daughter that he actioned it. He does support every day. And again, this goes back to that level of humility and companies really taking on the ethos of their founder.
turns.zh: 我倒吸一口凉气说：“好吧，我的 DoorDash 生涯就这样结束了。” 但托尼很棒。他说：“嘿，爱丽丝，我们这儿有送货员送了好几个月、好几年的，他们一直给我反馈。这是你最近给我的最有价值的反馈，而你才送过几次而已。” 等我们到家时，他已经给产品团队发邮件指出问题，提出改进建议。他们当时已经在处理了。这显示了 DoorDash 的行动导向精神，以及对客户的执着态度。托尼做客户支持并不罕见。不是因为听了我女儿的话才行动的，他每天都在支持用户。这又回到了那种谦逊的态度，公司真正践行创始人的理念。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What an awesome story. I want to chat a bit more about the, what is it called? WeDash? Is that the program?
turns.zh: 真是个精彩的故事。我想再聊聊那个项目叫什么？WeDash 吗？

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah.
turns.zh: 对，对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So you say that you're supposed to do it how many times a year, four times a year?
turns.zh: 你说一年要做几次，四次？

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: Yeah, at least four times a year.
turns.zh: 对，一年至少四次。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then you said that you do it a lot more often. How often are you doing it? And then, is there any other fun stories of that experience, someone like you delivering someone's sandwich?
turns.zh: 那你实际做得更频繁。你大概一个月一次？还有其他有趣的经历吗？比如你给别人送三明治？

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: I probably do it once a month.
turns.zh: 我大概一个月一次。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇哦。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: And there, there's all kinds of great WeDash stories, but I don't know how interesting they're going to be to the broader public because, for me, it's just about getting out and experiencing the product. I almost always find something that's broken, and I send an email to... We have a Slack channel that's devoted to experiences via WeDash. It's everything from, I found a bug once where it wasn't routing you necessarily the fastest route. It was going using straight line as opposed to road. That was something that we fixed. And for me, the best parts about WeDash are the experiences, the interactions with the restaurants, the interactions with colleagues. So I'll go delivering with Ryan Sokol, the head of engineering. I'll give him a hard time about refining the product and things like that. But that's, by far, my favorite WeDash story, is the one with my daughter.
turns.zh: 还有各种 WeDash 的精彩故事，但我不知道这些对公众有多大吸引力，因为对我来说，就是去体验产品。我几乎每次都能发现问题，给团队发邮件……我们有一个专门讨论 WeDash 体验的 Slack 频道。比如有次发现路线规划不合理，用直线路线而不是道路路线，这个问题后来解决了。对我来说，WeDash 最棒的部分是体验、与餐厅的互动、与同事的交流。所以我会和工程部主管瑞安·索科尔一起送货，逗他优化产品之类的。但迄今为止，我最喜欢的 WeDash 故事，还是和女儿的那次。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a good one. So at Airbnb, we actually had a similar program, where Brian wanted everyone to be a host on Airbnb. But as you can imagine, that's much harder. Not everyone is able to. Not everyone has a place to. So it's always kind of a challenge to make people do that. I imagine DoorDash is a lot easier because a lot of people can go around and deliver things. But yeah, such a killer idea, such a good way of dogfooding your product.
turns.zh: 真是个好主意。在Airbnb，我们其实也曾推行过类似的项目，布莱恩希望每个人都能成为Airbnb的房东。但你可以想象，这要难得多——不是每个人都能做到，也不是每个人都有房源可供出租。因此，要让人们参与这种活动总是颇具挑战。我想DoorDash要容易得多，因为很多人都能外出送货。但确实是个绝妙的创意，也是让产品自我验证的绝佳方式。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: Yeah, it's a good point, but not everyone is able, for a host of reasons, at DoorDash to do it. And so there are alternatives. So you can do customer support, for example, in lieu of actually going and doing deliveries. It's just about making people have empathy and get closer to the product. It's also, going back to the culture point you raise, it's a great way to weed out people that maybe we wouldn't want to work with, right, because not every software engineer wants to hop in their Tesla and go out and deliver McDonald's to some kids. Right? It takes a certain level of humility, a certain amount of customer obsession, to even sign up for that. So we're really vocal during the interview process that this is something that's expected. And it serves as a governor to attract the people that we think are going to be most successful at the company.
turns.zh: 没错，这点很对，但在DoorDash，并非所有人都能因种种原因参与其中。所以会有替代方案。比如，你可以从事客户支持工作，而不是亲自去送货。关键在于让人们对产品有同理心，更贴近产品。这也回到了你提到的文化要点——这也是筛选出不适合我们公司的人的好方法，毕竟不是每个软件工程师都愿意跳进特斯拉，为孩子们送麦当劳，对吧？这需要一定的谦逊精神和以客户为中心的理念，才能愿意参与这样的项目。因此，我们在面试过程中会明确强调这是必备的素质。它还能有效吸引那些我们认为最有可能在公司取得成功的人才。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. Imagine all your programs have the Dash in there somewhere. Something Dash.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个主意。想象一下，你的所有项目名称里都带有“Dash”元素。比如“Dash”之类的。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: We try. I think when I was head of a marketing, we did a much worse job. I think we're doing much better now.
turns.zh: 我们一直在努力。我记得我担任市场总监时，我们做得更糟糕。现在我们做得好多了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Nice. And Airbnb, it was always Air Something. Okay. So, I think one of the most interesting things about you and your background, and maybe unusual things, is the number of teams that you've led over your time at DoorDash. I have a list here. So over your time at DoorDash, you've led the HR team. You've led the customer support team, led the sales team, the marketing team. Now you lead the BD and corp dev team. Initially, I think, you were chief legal officer. So here's my question. As someone that, I imagine, doesn't have a ton of expertise and experience in a lot of these areas, how are you able to credibly lead these teams? And I ask partly because as a founder, you have to learn how to lead teams and people that you don't actually know what they're doing as well as they do. And so I'm just curious what you've learned about being able to lead teams in such disparate skill sets and functions.
turns.zh: 不错。Airbnb一直都是“Air Something”。好的。我觉得你和你的背景中最有趣、或许也最不寻常的地方，就是你在DoorDash任职期间领导的团队数量之多。我这里有一份清单。在DoorDash任职期间，你领导过人力资源团队、客户支持团队、销售团队、市场团队。现在你领导商务开发和企业发展团队。最初，我想你应该是首席法务官吧。所以我的问题是，作为一个在很多这些领域缺乏专业知识和经验的人，你是如何能够可信地领导这些团队的？我这么问部分原因是，作为创始人，你必须学会如何领导那些你并不真正了解其工作内容却比他们自己更擅长的人。因此，我很好奇你是如何在如此不同的技能组合和职能中领导团队的。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: Yeah, the one thing I'll say is, I did not run sales. That's maybe one of the very few non-technical functions I did not lead. But the question is a good one. And I had massive imposter syndrome the first time Tony asked me to take on something that I wasn't a subject matter expert in. And I told him I didn't want to do it. And he had me read this book called Range by David Epstein. And the general thesis is that generalists are better than specialists. And it goes through all these examples of about how Nobel Prize winners are usually amazing in something other than the field that they actually win the Nobel Prize in.
turns.zh: 是的，我要说的是，我没有负责过销售。这或许是我唯一没有领导过的非技术部门。但你的问题很好。当托尼第一次让我接手一个我并非主题专家的领域时，我有很严重的冒名顶替综合症。我告诉他我不想做。但他让我读了大卫·爱泼斯坦的《全能人才》一书。书中核心观点是通才比专家更出色。书中举了许多例子，比如诺贝尔奖得主通常在诺贝尔奖获奖领域之外的其他领域也表现出色。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: And Tony believes pretty deeply in this philosophy, and the way he explained it to me is as follows. If you want to achieve a 10x outcome, hiring someone that's an expert in the field, it's maybe unlikely you're going to achieve that 10x outcome, because they're likely to do things the way things have always been done. So you might achieve incremental benefits, but the odds of completely reinventing the system and doing something that's vastly superior to others is much lower. And he said, "I know you don't know how to do this stuff. That's why I'm putting you in the role." And I said, "Okay."
turns.zh: 托尼对这种理念深信不疑，他向我解释道：如果你想获得10倍的成果，雇佣某个领域的专家或许不太可能实现这一目标，因为他们很可能沿用传统做法。因此，你或许能获得一些增量效益，但彻底重塑系统、创造超越他人的卓越成果的可能性则微乎其微。他曾对我说："我知道你不擅长这些事务。所以我才让你担任这个角色。"我回答："好的。"

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: So, first thing he helped me do was believe that I could add value here. And then, the second thing for me was to go out and find the best people that really were the subject matter experts, and add the value I could to help them be successful. And I found that they were actually really attracted to wanting to work with someone like me, who came into the interview process and said, "Good news, bad news. I don't know your field anywhere near as well as you do. Here's the ways I intend to help you. Here's what I think you can provide. And at the end of the day, I'm going to get out of your way." And that's really proven true. So, I ran marketing. Hired initially a head of brand, Kofi, who now is our CMO. Hired ahead of legal, who's now our GC, Tia Sherringham. And these people have really just excelled at their function and, with the warmup that I was able to provide, have really proven that they're much better at the jobs than I was.
turns.zh: 首先，托尼帮助我相信自己能在这里创造价值。接下来，我需要去寻找真正是领域专家的顶尖人才，并尽我所能为他们助力成功。我发现，他们其实很乐意与像我这样的人合作——我参加面试时会说："好消息是，我在你们的领域远不及你们精通。但我会用以下方式为你们提供帮助……"最后，我会退居幕后。这确实成效显著。比如，我负责市场营销部门时，最初聘请的品牌负责人科菲如今已晋升为首席营销官；提前招聘的法务负责人蒂娅·谢林汉姆如今已成为首席法务官。这些人都出色地完成了本职工作，而我提供的助力支持也让他们比我更胜一筹。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You don't strike me as someone that is trying to build empires and take over all these teams. I imagine this kind of came at you because you've been doing a great job at other things. Is that how it worked? And, I guess, is there anything, any lessons there that you can take away?
turns.zh: 你给人的感觉不像是想建立商业帝国、接管所有团队。我猜这多半是因为你在其他领域表现出色才获得了这样的机会。对吧？你能否总结一下从中汲取的经验教训？

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: Yeah, hundred percent. I run a 12-person org today. So I've gone from running 1,500 people in the company to 12. And for me, people talk a lot about hiring people better than you are. People don't talk a lot about what you do when you hire those people. And if you really care about the company and your long-term brand as an individual, as a manager, you realize what you want to do when you find the person that's better than you is you want to slowly get out of the way. And it's really good for the company. It's my favorite part of my job, is seeing people that either I've hired or managed be successful on their own.
turns.zh: 完全赞同。我现在管理的团队只有12人。从管理1500人的团队到管理12人的团队，转变巨大。人们常说要雇佣比自己更优秀的人，却很少谈到雇到这些人后该怎么做。如果你真正关心公司和个人长期品牌价值，作为管理者，你会意识到，当你找到比自己更优秀的人时，最该做的事就是逐渐退居幕后。这对公司大有裨益。看到自己招募或管理的人能独当一面，是我工作中最有成就感的部分。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: And I think it's a big part of our success, is this desire to be successful, regardless of who's in charge. And that comes from the fact when I joined DoorDash, we were getting our tails kicked. We were in fourth place in the space. Uber had just launched food and rocket to market share leadership. And I think that was really good for us as a company because we realized unless we all worked together, and it wasn't about who was doing what or things like that, we weren't going to have a shot at being successful. And I think that ethos has really pervaded and persisted since then.
turns.zh: 我认为，我们成功的关键在于无论谁负责，都渴望取得成功。这源于我加入DoorDash时的困境——当时我们在行业中排名第四，优步刚推出外卖业务并迅速占据市场领先地位。这对我们公司意义重大，因为我们意识到，如果不齐心协力，不论分工如何，都没有成功的机会。自那以后，这种企业精神就深深根植于公司文化中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I think most people don't realize DoorDash actually has the biggest market share in food delivery. Imagine that's still true. I've always seen these line charts of market share, and DoorDash is always the top. And I think people kind of think Uber Eats is winning, but it's not true.
turns.zh: 是啊。我觉得大多数人都没意识到DoorDash实际上在外卖配送市场占据着最大的份额。假设这种情况属实的话。我见过的市场份额图表中，DoorDash总是位居榜首。人们可能认为Uber Eats正在胜出，但事实并非如此。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: Yeah, I mean, the category charts I've seen are consistent with what you said by a pretty wide margin. But we try not to focus on things like that. We try to focus on the customer experience. And it's humbling in our space because we're doing millions and millions and millions of deliveries a day, and those deliveries will go wrong, no matter how hard you try. And we read those experiences. We do customer support, and we understand that there's a long ways to go. So we're just getting started, and we know that.
turns.zh: 是的，我是指我见过的类别图表与你所说的基本一致。但我们尽量不去关注这些数据，而是专注于客户体验。在我们这个领域，这很令人谦卑，因为我们每天要处理数百万次配送任务，无论你怎么努力，总会有差错发生。我们会认真阅读用户反馈，提供客户支持，并深知还有很长的路要走。所以我们才刚刚起步，对此心知肚明。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You mentioned that you ran this 1,500-person org at one point, and something that I've heard you do, that helps you do that, is you have this document that you put together that kind of explains how to work with Keith, and also, just broadly, how things work at DoorDash. Can you talk about this document, and why you thought it was necessary, and kind of the impact something like this has had? And then we're going to share a link to a redacted version of this in the show notes.
turns.zh: 你提到自己曾管理过一个1500人的团队，我听说你有一份文件，能有效帮助你管理团队。这份文件主要讲解如何与基思（Keith）合作，以及DoorDash的整体运作机制。能否谈谈这份文件的意义、你为何认为它必要，以及它产生了哪些影响？稍后我们会在节目笔记中分享一份经编辑的版本链接。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: One thing I've learned is it's super hard to scale culture, especially when you're growing as fast as DoorDash has since I joined. We were two or three X'ing the company, from a head count perspective, for the vast majority of my time every year. And so one thing I noticed is, it's hard to come into a place and be new and understand how things work and what it means to be successful there. And so the idea was to do our best to scale that. And one thing that Tony taught me is one thing that scales really well is written work [inaudible 00:19:16]. And so I put together this document. There's three basic subject matters. It's my expectations slash what I've seen as traits in successful people within the company.
turns.zh: 我学到的一点是，文化的扩展极其困难，尤其是在DoorDash这样快速发展的公司里。我加入以来，每年绝大多数时间里，公司规模都以两到三倍的速度增长。因此，我发现新加入的员工很难理解公司的运作方式和成功的标准。于是我们的目标是尽可能扩大这种文化的覆盖范围。托尼教会我的一点是，书面指导能极大促进文化传播[00:19:16未录音]。基于此，我整理了这份文件，内容主要分为三个板块：我的期望与公司内成功人士的共性特征。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: Two are how I can improve, like basically, feedback I've gotten in things I'm working on. For example, I'm a litigator by training, and so I tend to argue about things, even if I agree with people to the test levels of conviction. And I got feedback from my team that was really confusing because I'd be arguing against something, and then we would execute that exact thing. And so I try to be transparent about that and explain how I work through problems, but also in saying, "Hey, this is something I'm trying to improve on, is not being quite so argumentative for sport." And then it talks about what my commitments are to team. So, "I'm committed to finding you your next job even if that's not at DoorDash. Life's too short to be in a job you don't like," things like that.
turns.zh: 第二部分是自我提升，比如我对工作的反馈。例如，我曾是一名诉讼律师，所以即使在内心深处认同他人观点，也倾向于争论不休。团队反馈让我困惑不已——明明我反对某个方案，结果我们却照做了。所以我会坦诚地解释自己的工作方式，同时说明：“嘿，我正在努力改进，别再为了争论而争论了。” 文件还提到了我对团队的承诺，比如“即使不在DoorDash，我也会帮你找到下一份工作”，因为“人生太短暂了，别待在自己不喜欢的岗位上”。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've heard from a few people how impactful this document ended up being. I guess, what impact have you seen this have on the org that you've run in the company and then, yeah, any other examples of just why this is powerful? Because I imagine some people listening are like, "Oh, I should do something like this."
turns.zh: 我听几个人说这份文件产生了巨大影响。请问它对你的团队产生了哪些具体影响？你能否举例说明其强大之处？因为我想有些听众可能会想：“哦，我也应该做这样的事。”

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: Yeah, I mean, for me, one of an executive's main jobs is to attract and retain top talent. And going back to why people have joined DoorDash, Kofi Amoo-Gottfried, who's now our CMO, joined me as head of brand when I was running marketing. And it's comical because this person is a legend in the marketing space, and I had no idea what was going on. And so convincing him to join, I was really nervous about. And the point where he decided to join, I had sent him this document. He wanted to know what it was like to work with me. I said, "Well, I've actually written that down."
turns.zh: 是的，我觉得对高管来说，吸引和留住顶尖人才是他们的主要职责之一。再说回人们加入DoorDash的原因。现任首席营销官科菲·阿莫-戈特弗里德（Kofi Amoo-Gottfried）在我负责营销部门时，曾以品牌主管的身份加入我的团队。说起来挺有趣的，他在营销界是个传奇人物，而我当时却对此一无所知。所以要说服他加入，我真的很紧张。在他决定加入的那一刻，我给他发了一份文件。他想了解和我共事的感觉。我说：“嗯，我其实已经把这些写下来了。”

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: And he later told me that that was a really important factor for him, that someone was so transparent about their areas for growth, how they thought they could be helpful, and he liked the fact that I knew that I didn't know. And so he knew he was going to have a lot of autonomy on the role, and that was really important to him. But more broadly within the organization, how it's been helpful is just being able to have people engage with me in a way, and with the company in a way that is so consistent with the culture from day one. I've had people come and tell me, that I'd never met before, that they'd read the doc, even if they're on a different team, and just how helpful it's been to try to acclimate to this fast-paced environment, where you're learning while drinking from the fire hose, effectively.
turns.zh: 后来他告诉我，这对他来说是个很重要的考量因素——有人能如此坦诚地谈论自己的成长空间，谈论自己能如何提供帮助。他欣赏我承认自己有所不足的做法。他知道自己在这份工作中会有很大的自主权，这对他来说非常重要。但更广泛地说，在整个组织内部，这样做的好处在于能让员工以一种与公司文化从一开始就高度契合的方式与我以及公司互动。我曾遇到过一些人，虽然之前从未谋面，但他们读过那份文件，即使他们在不同的团队工作，也能很好地适应这种快节奏的环境，在边做边学的过程中快速成长。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, that makes sense. Touching a little bit on it, you talked about all these amazing people you've led and how you've been able to do that. Something else I've heard that you do that's pretty unusual is you help people that you manage find their next job, which may not necessarily be within the company, maybe at another company. You kind of help them land it and find something else to do. I've never heard of that before, really. I'd love to hear why you decided to do that, how you do that, and just the kind of impact, second-order impact, maybe, that has, maybe that leads you to be doing this.
turns.zh: 是啊，这说得通。再稍微谈谈这个话题，你提到了你领导过很多优秀的人才，以及你是如何做到的。我还听说你做过一件很不寻常的事，就是帮助你手下的人寻找下一份工作——不一定非要在公司内部，可能在其他公司。你会帮助他们成功跳槽，找到新的发展机会。我还从未听说过这种做法，真的很想听听你为什么会这样做，具体怎么做的，以及这可能带来的哪些连锁反应，比如是否因此获得了更高的认可。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: It wasn't a calculated decision why I started doing it. Then I gave it a lot of thought because I was afraid that I might get some blowback when people started taking jobs elsewhere. And as I thought about it, I realized it really is better for the company to have that type of open dialogue with people that work on your team. I think that's true for a few reasons. In this "How to work with Keith" document, I say, "I will help you find your next job." And what that means is, number one, people are going to be transparent with you, or more transparent, if they're looking for something else or if they're not happy. That's going to allow you to lay the foundation for a backfill so you're much less likely to get surprised when someone leaves.
turns.zh: 我最初开始这么做并非经过深思熟虑。后来我仔细考虑过，因为担心当人们跳槽到其他公司时可能会产生负面反应。深入思考后，我意识到与团队成员保持开放对话对公司更有益。这有几个原因。在《如何与基思共事》这份文件中，我写道：“我会帮助你找到下一份工作。”这意味着：首先，人们会对你更加坦诚——如果他们在寻找新的机会，或者对现状不满，他们会更坦诚。这能为你未来的人员补位奠定基础，当有人离职时，你就不太可能措手不及了。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: Number two, what's going to happen is if someone runs a blind reference on me at this point with someone that I've managed, which in the current environment is more and more common, people diligencing the managers, what they're going to hear is, "Keith's going to put you first." And I think that's really motivating for a lot of people. So if you're thinking on a five-, 10-year horizon of your career as a manager, whether you're an entrepreneur hiring people into your company, whether you're a product manager who's trying to build a team, building that long-term reputation, I think people take much too shortsighted perspective on that.
turns.zh: 接下来要说的是，假如有人在我这里匿名推荐某位我曾管理过的人——在当前的环境下，这种对管理者的审查越来越常见——对方听到的评价会是：“基思会把你放在首位。”我认为这对很多人来说非常有激励作用。所以如果你以五年、十年的职业生涯规划来看，无论你是招聘人才的创业者，还是试图组建团队的产品经理，树立长远声誉至关重要。但人们对此的考虑往往过于短视。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: And so now if I get a blind reference, people are going to hear that, "It's not all about the company. It's not all about Keith. It's about you and your career," and that's going to pay back 10x. Maybe you lose one really talented person, but they probably shouldn't be there anyway. They're probably going to leave anyway. And this way, you can participate in that and really drive value for them, as well as for the company in the future, by creating a much better reputation for the group of managers. So it's been really helpful for me. I keep in touch with a lot of people who have left, and we get a lot of boomerangs, too. There's a lot of people who leave DoorDash and come back. And that's something I love seeing because it shows that people have gone out and seen what else is out there and realized this is the right place for them.
turns.zh: 如今如果有人匿名推荐我，人们会听到：“这不全是关于公司的，也不全是关于基思的，而是关于你和你的职业生涯的。” 这种做法能带来十倍的回报。或许你会失去一位才华横溢的人，但他们可能本来就不该留在这里。他们迟早会离开。通过这种方式，你能参与其中，为他们和公司创造长期价值，同时提升管理团队的声誉。这对我来说非常有效。我和许多离职员工保持联系，也有很多回流人才。很多人离开DoorDash后又回来了。看到这些让我很欣慰，因为这表明人们出去看看外面的机会后，意识到这里才是适合他们的地方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Can you talk a bit about how you operationalize this? Because this is just out there. "Tell me if you're thinking about a new job, and I will talk to you through your options and help you find something." Or is there anything else there for folks that maybe want to offer this to their employees?
turns.zh: 你能谈谈如何具体实施吗？因为这听起来挺抽象的。“如果你在考虑新工作，告诉我，我会帮你分析选择，帮你找到合适的机会。” 或者有没有其他方法可以提供给员工？

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: So, first of all, I put it in this document. And so I say how I run one-on-ones in my "how to work with Keith" document, and the last 10 minutes of my one-on-ones are career development conversations. That's a really fertile ground for having the discussion. But for particularly more senior folks, if I get pinged for a GC job, or when I would get pinged by a recruiter for a GC job, I would forward that to Tia Sherringham, who's now our general counsel but was basically head of legal for years before she got the general counsel title. And I'd say, "Hey, Tia, I don't know when this job's going to be available here. I'm still liking what I'm doing. I think I'm still adding value. If you think it's time for you to leave, I think this is a really good opportunity."
turns.zh: 首先，我把这些内容写进了我的《如何与基思共事》文档。在一对一会议的最后10分钟，我会进行职业发展讨论，这是一个很好的沟通机会。但对于更资深的员工，如果有人联系我推荐总法律顾问职位，或者招聘人员主动推荐时，我会把信息转交给蒂娅·谢林汉姆。她现在是我们的总法律顾问，但在获得总法律顾问头衔之前，她多年担任法律部主管。我会说：“蒂娅，我不知道这个职位何时空缺。我仍然热爱现在的工作，也认为自己能创造价值。如果你觉得是时候离开了，这确实是个好机会。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, that's [inaudible 00:25:12].
turns.zh: 哇，真是令人惊叹（00:25:12处语音不清）。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: And I say, in addition to that, "You're going to learn the questions they asked during the interview process. You're going to learn what type of qualifications they're looking for. And if I'm not getting you that experience, you can tell me." And thankfully for me, Tia decided to stay and has now grown into the general counsel of DoorDash, and doing a much better job at the role than I ever did. But she had the opportunity to leave, and I think she learned from some of those in-bounds and the experiences she had.
turns.zh: 除此之外，我还会说：“你将了解面试过程中他们提问的问题，了解他们所寻求的资质要求。如果我没有给你这样的经验，你可以告诉我。” 幸运的是，蒂娅决定留下，如今已成长为DoorDash的总法律顾问，胜任这份工作的表现远超我的预期。但她曾有机会离开，我想她从这些接触和经历中吸取了教训。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. That's amazing, that your bosses forward you recruiter pitches to go work somewhere else.
turns.zh: 哇。你的上司把招聘信息转交给你，让你去别的地方工作，这真是太不可思议了。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: Think it made her want to stay. Right? If I wasn't invested in her success, she could have left any time and gotten a job, super qualified. But I think she felt a sense of loyalty based on my sense of loyalty, and I think it worked out best for all involved.
turns.zh: 觉得这让她想留下来。对吧？如果我不关心她的成功，她随时可能离开，找份超有资质的工作。但我觉得她基于我的忠诚感产生了归属感，我认为这对各方来说都是最好的结果。

turns.en: I love it. This episode is brought to you by Coda. turns.zh: 我太喜欢这集了。本期节目由Coda赞助。你们听我说过，Coda是能整合所有信息的工具，能帮助团队更高效地运作。我深有体会，因为Coda就是为我做到这些的。我每天都用Coda来整理我的通讯内容日历、播客采访笔记，还协调赞助商事宜。最近，我甚至写了一篇关于Coda产品团队如何运作的文章。在那篇文章里，他们分享了内部使用的十几个模板，包括路线图管理、OKR流程、内部反馈收集。实际上，他们的整个产品开发流程都是在Coda中完成的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something else I hear about you, which I'm sensing as we chat more and more, and I could see why this is true, is that on the DoorDash kind of C-suite and board meeting and board in general, you play this really strong unifying force that helps the group come to fast decisions on really complicated topics. And I'm curious. One, would you agree with that? And two, what is it that you do that helps a lot of strongly opinionated people come to decisions on really complicated decisions?
turns.zh: 我从你身上听说了另一件事，通过我们的深入交谈，我能理解这是真的。在DoorDash的C级高管会议和董事会会议上，你扮演着强有力的凝聚角色，帮助团队在复杂议题上快速达成决策。我很好奇。一，你是否认同这一点？二，你是如何帮助众多固执己见的人在复杂议题上达成共识的？

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: I hope that's true. I think that, for me, it all comes down to empathy. And what I mean by that is, you have to understand what different people's motivations are in the room. Different people are goaled on different things. People come from different life experiences and different work experiences. And I think it's really important to make each person feel heard. We had a situation, for example, where we were deciding between a trade-off between two business lines. It was a profitability question for one business line, to make one business line much more profitable to do a certain partnership, but it would come at the expense of the growth of another business line that was more nascent.
turns.zh: 我希望这是真的。对我来说，关键在于同理心。我的意思是，你必须理解房间里不同人的动机。不同的人有不同的目标。人们来自不同的生活经历和工作经历。我认为让每个人都感受到被倾听非常重要。比如，我们曾在两个业务线之间的权衡问题上做决策。一个业务线面临盈利问题，通过某项合作能大幅提升盈利，但代价是牺牲另一个尚在起步阶段的业务线的增长。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: And so it's hard when you get the GMs for all these businesses together, and they have very strong perspectives and good reasons on both sides about why path A is better profitability, path B is better for growth. And they're arguing very strenuously, in part because they want to hit their numbers, in part because they believe it. One thing I found super effective in those contexts is I try to ask the other side. So, let's take the profitability side. I ask them to make the growth case. I say, "Tell me the three best reasons why we should actually focus on growth here." That generates instant empathy for the other side. And sometimes, they'll even persuade themselves as they're talking and say, "I think you're right that we should focus on growth here. We can achieve this profitability measure later" or vice versa. And so generating empathy and having empathy for the other side, understanding how they're goaled and what they're bringing to the conversation, I think is the first step to having those really tough conversations.
turns.zh: 因此，当你把所有这些业务的总经理们聚在一起时，情况就很棘手了。他们在路径A更能提升盈利能力、路径B更有助于增长这两个问题上都有着非常坚定的观点，并且他们会激烈争辩——部分原因是为了达成业绩目标，部分则出于真心信念。在这种情况下，我发现一个非常有效的策略，就是反问对方。比如，针对盈利派，我会让他们先阐述增长的理由。我会说：“请告诉我三个最有力的理由，说明我们为何应该专注于增长。”这样做能立即激发对方的共鸣。有时，他们在陈述过程中甚至会自我说服，说：“我觉得你说得对，我们确实应该把重点放在增长上。盈利目标可以稍后再达成。”反之亦然。建立共情、理解对方的立场和诉求，才是开展艰难对话的第一步。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. What other steps are there? I like that as a first step. Is there anything else you have that you end up finding is really helpful there?
turns.zh: 这主意不错。还有哪些步骤呢？把这当作第一步很明智。还有其他实用的方法吗？

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: Sometimes these conversations can go on forever. Right? People just want to keep going back to an argument they've already made, because they're not willing to settle, and there needs to be someone that says, "All right. We got to be clear on who the decision maker is here. If we haven't reached a consensus, who's the tiebreaker?" And a lot of time that's our CEO, Tony Xu, but a lot of times it's the GM for a certain business line or a head of product or a head of engineering, depending on the decision to be made. I think being really clear about, "Hey, we're all going to come together. We're going to have a healthy debate. We're going to make sure everyone's perspectives are heard. We're going to try to reach consensus, but the end of the day, here's the person that's going to make the decision, and we're going to make it on this time horizon. And once the decision is made, we're going to [inaudible 00:30:16]."
turns.zh: 有些讨论可能会没完没了。对吧？人们总想回到自己已提出的论点，因为不愿妥协。这时就需要有人说：“好吧，我们得明确谁是决策者。若无法达成共识，谁来打破僵局？” 通常是我们的CEO徐东，但有时是某个业务线的总经理、产品负责人或工程主管，视具体决策而定。我认为关键在于明确：大家齐聚一堂，展开健康辩论，确保各方观点被听取，努力达成共识，但最终由某人做出决策，且必须在既定时间框架内完成。一旦决策确定，就必须[00:30:16未录音]。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: And I think that having someone that's in the room that has run a lot of the functions that are trying to articulate the perspective is helpful, and someone who's been at the company as long as I have and given up as much as I have... Right? To your point earlier, everyone knows I'm not trying to build an empire. I'm trying to find a way to win. And I think it gives me some credibility to call the question, figure out who decision maker is, set a time line, and move on. The only way it works is if there's empathy on both sides.
turns.zh: 会场上若有参与过多个职能部门、能清晰阐述各方观点，自然更有帮助。像我这样在公司深耕多年，又付出诸多心血的人……对吧？正如你之前所说，我无意建造帝国，只想找到取胜之道。因此，我有权发起质疑、明确决策者、设定时间节点并推进进程。但这一切的前提是双方都要心怀共情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is great, so I just took a few notes. One is there's essentially the steel man component. Have them steel man the other side, argue why that's the better decision. Clarify a decision maker. Make it clear like, "There's the tiebreaker. If we can't get there, this person's going to make the decision." And then create a time horizon of like, "We need to make a decision by this time." Is there anything else, before we move on to a different question?
turns.zh: 太棒了，我刚记了几个要点：本质上就是“换位思考”的过程。让对方从对方的角度去阐述更优的决策。明确决策者。说明“若无法达成共识，由此人做出决策”。然后设定时间节点：“我们必须在此时间点前做出决定。” 还有其他要点吗？我们接着讨论下一个问题。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: I think that's the right framework. I can tell you're product guy. You're very good at distilling it down to the essence. I think that's a good summary.
turns.zh: 我觉得这就是正确的框架。我看得出你是个产品人。你很善于提炼核心要点。这是个很好的总结。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, you got to do it. You mentioned the one-on-one meetings. And I took a note on this, actually, and I wanted to come back to it. You mentioned at the end of your one-on-one meetings you have this kind of coaching career conversation. Is there anything else you could share about just your approach to one-on-one meetings, your agenda or how you think about one-on-ones?
turns.zh: 是的，你必须这么做。你提到了那些一对一的会议。实际上，我对此做了笔记，还想再深入探讨一下。你提到在一对一会议结束时，会进行那种关于职业发展的对话。关于一对一会议的具体方法、议程安排或思路，还有什么可以分享的吗？

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: This is super tactical. It's something I think is really important, is I'm very clear, in the document we talked about earlier, about how I like to work, is I demand feedback for me. And so we set aside time during one-on-ones where I want the feedback. First, constructive feedback. And I expect it, and if you don't give it to me, I'm going to press you on constructive feedback. And then I give feedback. I tell this to managers all the time. If you create a space where you require constructive feedback, it's a lot easier to give feedback. One of the top things I hear from managers, especially new managers, they don't like giving constructive feedback. They want to be positive. They want to be liked and things like that. And so it's a nice way to create space to have that dialogue.
turns.zh: 这非常有技巧性。我认为这很重要。在我们之前讨论的文件里，我明确说明了自己的工作方式——我需要得到反馈。所以在一对一会议中，我们会专门留出时间收集反馈。首先是建设性的反馈。我期望得到这样的反馈，如果你不给出，我会追问。然后我再给出反馈。我一直告诫管理者，如果你创造出一个需要建设性反馈的环境，收集反馈就会容易得多。很多新晋管理者跟我抱怨，他们不喜欢给出建设性反馈，只想保持积极，讨人喜欢之类的。所以建立这样的对话空间很重要。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: And that's something I actually learned from Travis, when I was at Uber. We had a system called T3 B3, where during reviews or pulse check-ins, you'd have to say three positives about your manager and three constructive pieces of feedback for your manager. And the first time I did it, I just did the T, the tough things, for my manager, who was the general counsel at the time. And Travis came over, and, "This is totally unacceptable. You have to provide constructive feedback," which made me super uncomfortable but created the right environment, where people could have these tough conversations because, "My manager can't get mad at me, because she knows the CEO's going to come give me a hard time if I don't provide some constructive feedback." And I think having that as an expectation is super important to building open lines of communication.
turns.zh: 这点我是在Uber时从特拉维斯那里学到的。我们有个叫T3 B3的系统，在评估或脉搏检查时，要对上级说三个优点和三个建设性意见。第一次我只对当时的总法律顾问提了三个建设性意见，特拉维斯就过来说：“这完全不可接受。你必须给出建设性反馈。”这让我很不自在，但确实营造了正确的环境，因为“我的上级不能生我的气，因为如果我不给出反馈，CEO会找我麻烦。”我认为这种期望对建立开放的沟通渠道非常重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. I like this T3 B3. So T is top good things and B is three bad things.
turns.zh: 哇。我喜欢这个T3 B3系统。T是三个优点，B是三个缺点。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. I'm trying to imagine you in this meeting with the CMO you mentioned, and them having to give you constructive feedback. That's always hard, even though you expect it. Is there anything else you do to help people feel comfortable giving you hard feedback in meetings like that?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我试着想象你和提到的首席营销官开会，他们必须给你建设性反馈。这总是很难的，即使你期待得到反馈。你还有什么方法能让人们在这种会议上更自在地给你负面反馈吗？

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: You have to thank them for it. Right? I mean, there's a saying, "Feedback is a gift," but you have to say stuff, and you have to action. And that's one thing I've found that can be really demotivating for folks. A lot of these companies have these pulse surveys, or they talk about what the company can do better, and they put the results on the screen, and, "We're going to work on it," and that's the end of it.
turns.zh: 你得感谢他们对你的反馈。是吧，有句话说“反馈是礼物”，但你得采取行动。我发现这对人们很打击士气。很多公司做脉搏调查，或者谈论公司可以改进的地方，把结果展示出来，然后说“我们会改进”，然后就结束了。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: And that was something I learned early on at DoorDash that people didn't like, unless you were going to come back and say, "Hey, this was our lowest performing area in the pulse survey. Here are the three things we did to action it," because that's how you would treat the business. Right? If we got feedback from a customer or from another business line, you would say, "Heard it. We're going to come back and report out on what we're going to do differently, and then we're going to track the progress." And so I think that's really important when you receive feedback. You have to show people that you're actioning it and say, "I heard this from you. Checking in. Am I doing better? Here are the things that I've changed." And so making sure that there's that feedback loop, I think, is another important part of creating the right structure for a good, healthy culture.
turns.zh: 这是我在DoorDash早期就领悟到的一个道理——除非你能回过头来对员工说：“嘿，用户调查中你们表现最差的领域在这里。以下是我们为此采取的三项改进措施。”否则没人会买账。因为这才是正确的企业管理之道。比如，当我们收到客户或其他业务部门的反馈时，我们会说：“收到了，我们会回来汇报改进措施，并持续跟进进展。”所以我认为，当接到反馈时，必须向大家表明你在积极行动，并说：“我听到了你们的意见。现在来跟进一下，我做得是否更好了？以下是我做出的改变。” 保持这种反馈循环，才是构建健康文化的关键。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Another guest on the podcast had the same exact advice for getting feedback, and the way he described it is you want to be enthusiastic about like, "Thank you so much for that." And the way he described it is even though you're melting inside because you don't want to hear, "Thank you so much. That was so helpful."
turns.zh: 播客中另一位嘉宾给出的获取反馈的建议也如出一辙。他强调要热情回应：“非常感谢您的反馈。”即便内心其实很崩溃，但表面仍要保持积极，说：“非常感谢您的反馈。这对我们帮助很大。”

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: It's really good advice.
turns.zh: 这确实是个很好的建议。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to zoom out a little bit and talk about the DoorDash kind of journey. There's been a lot of high highs with DoorDash. There's been some low lows. I know that there was a funding round at one point, where it was very precarious and may not have worked out. Question I have for you around that is just, leading through hardships and through tough times, what have you learned, as a leader, about how to lead through challenging times? And ask partly because a lot of companies are going through that right now. It's pretty hard for a lot of folks out there, a lot of layoffs. And so yeah, I'm curious what you've learned about leading through challenging times.
turns.zh: 我想稍微回顾一下DoorDash的发展历程。公司经历过辉煌时刻，也遭遇过低谷。我知道曾有一轮融资险些失败。关于如何在逆境中领导团队，我想请教您作为领导者，如何在挑战中保持方向？尤其是当下许多公司正经历类似困境，裁员潮席卷而来，对许多人来说日子艰难。您在领导力方面有何心得？

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: Yeah. I'm going to regurgitate some advice I got from some folks on our board at the same time, when we were having really tough times, which I really didn't like hearing at the time, but I was kind of new to the space. And that is, "Tough times make companies," for a host of reasons. I mean, this is super healthy for the start-ups out there right now. It's because, number one, you're going to find out who the mercenaries are on the team, that are people that are there for the mission, versus they're there because they think this is going to be a quick road to riches. We had a lot of people leave the company when Uber launched food, and we fell quickly behind. And that was good for us because the people that stayed were there because they wanted to work on this team, on this mission, and they really believed in it.
turns.zh: 是的。我要复述一下董事会成员在公司最艰难时期给我的建议。当时我听得很不爽，但毕竟初入行。这句话是：“逆境造就公司。” 有几个原因。比如，第一，你能识别出团队中的临时工——那些追随使命的人和追名逐利的人。在Uber推出外卖业务后，我们一度落后很多，许多人离职。但这反而是好事，因为留下来的人是真心想为这个团队、这个使命奋斗的。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: The second thing is it forces discipline. It's a good thing to focus on unit economics. And we didn't have the funding that a lot of our competitors did, which forced us to be super focused on our unit economics and efficient and serve the customer in unique ways from the start. And I think a lot of our success, even to this day, emanates from those tough times. The last thing I'll say is if you're a founder, and you're looking for talent, tough times are great because there's a lot more talent out there. I saw... I think it might have been Bill Gurley. Someone tweeted, "This is the best time in recent memory, since 2008, to start a company." And that really resonated with me because there's a lot of talented folks out there who are looking for their next thing. And three years ago, it was tough to find talent. And so I think there's a lot to like about tough times.
turns.zh: 接下来要说的是，它能促使我们保持纪律。专注于单位经济效益是一件好事。我们当时没有很多竞争对手所拥有的资金支持，这迫使我们从一开始就高度关注单位经济效益，保持高效，并以独特的方式为客户服务。我认为，我们至今取得的许多成功都源于那些艰难时期。最后我想说的是，如果你是一位创业者，正在寻找人才，艰难时期其实是绝佳的机会，因为人才市场上有很多优秀的人才在寻找下一个机遇。三年前，要找到人才还很困难。所以我认为艰难时期有很多值得珍视的地方。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: The last thing I'll say is, one thing that I found surprising is, from our surveys internally, people actually like crises at DoorDash. And I dug into that recently, and I was trying to figure out [inaudible 00:37:10] like these crises, and it's because there's singularity of focus. You know what the job is. You know you're going to get whatever resources the company has, when you're focused on the main thing. And these tough economic times will create that work. It's crystal clear. You got to cut, burn, and everyone's going to be doing what they need to do to achieve that outcome. And I think talented folks really like that, one, resourcing, and two, singularity of focus about what the main thing is. And crises manifests those for folks.
turns.zh: 最后我想说的是，我发现一个令人惊讶的现象——根据我们内部的调查，DoorDash的员工实际上喜欢危机时期。我最近深入研究了这个问题，试图理解这种现象背后的原因。关键在于，危机时期能让人专注于核心任务。大家清楚自己的职责所在，只要专注于核心任务，公司就会为你提供所需资源。经济低迷时期会迫使人们做出艰难选择，每个人都必须为实现目标付出必要努力。优秀的人才非常喜欢这种挑战，一是资源分配的清晰，二是专注于核心任务的清晰感。而危机时期恰恰能激发这些特质。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting that there's all these benefits to tough times. It's hard to recreate artificially. Reminds me a little bit of Frank Slootman, I think his name... and his book Amp It Up, where he talks a lot about the importance of urgency, always creating urgency. And obviously, a downturn like we have today is an urgent situation. Have you found that to be true, the power of creating urgency? And then, is there something you've learned about how to create that urgency at a company [inaudible 00:38:07]?
turns.zh: 有趣的是，艰难时期能带来诸多益处，但很难人为复制。这让我想起弗兰克·斯洛特曼（Frank Slootman），他在《Amp It Up》一书中强调紧迫感的重要性，永远创造紧迫感。显然，像我们现在面临的经济低迷就是一种紧迫情境。你是否也发现了创造紧迫感的力量？那么，在公司内部如何有效激发这种紧迫感呢？[00:38:07未录音]

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: Yeah, this is something Tony's talked about since the day I joined, and he's very good at, frustratingly good, at that, because just when you think you've achieved the goal, the goal might go up. It might get shorter if you're from the product side. And speaking specifically on the product, compound interest is a really hard concept to fully explain to people, to make them truly appreciate. But that's something Tony is fantastic at, which is, he understands that by pushing a road map up, even by a week, if you can continuously push up what you ship by a week, you're going to end up lapping competitors who are just one week behind because you're going to start the next thing a week sooner, and you're getting that 1.1, 1.01x return. And then it grows and grows and grows.
turns.zh: 是的，托尼从我加入公司那天起就一直在强调这一点，而且他在这方面做得极其出色，甚至可以说是令人沮丧的出色。因为当你以为已经达成目标时，目标可能又会提升。如果你来自产品部门，目标会变得更紧迫。具体到产品方面，复利效应是一个很难向人们充分解释、让他们真正领会的概念。但托尼在这方面堪称天才，他深知将路线图提前一周——哪怕只是一周——就能让产品迭代速度领先竞争对手一周，因为你能更早地启动下一个项目，从而获得1.1、1.01倍的回报。然后这种优势会不断叠加。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: And he's as good as I've ever seen, combined with our president, Christopher Payne, at creating that sense of urgency and just pushing people. "Do we really need to test this thing again or can we ship it? How can we move that much faster?" Even if it's by a small margin, understanding that you can compound those gains over time has been really impactful for our success.
turns.zh: 他和我们的总裁克里斯托弗·佩恩（Christopher Payne）一起，是我见过最善于营造紧迫感、推动团队前进的人。“我们真的需要再测试一次这个功能，还是可以直接上线？”“如何能更快地推进？”即使只是一点点进步，明白这些微小改进能随着时间累积成巨大优势，对我们的成功意义非凡。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I saw the same thing at Airbnb. It feels like, "Things are going well. Maybe we could take a little break," but it's constant just like, "How do we go faster? How do we go bigger? Okay, what's next? We launched this thing. Let's move on." And it feels like such a pattern across companies that do really well, is the founders continuing to keep that pressure on.
turns.zh: 我在Airbnb也看到了同样的情况。你会觉得，"一切进展顺利，或许我们可以稍作休息"，但现实却像是无休止地追问："我们如何能更快发展？如何能做得更大？好吧，下一步是什么？我们推出了这个新项目，现在继续前进吧。"这种模式在那些发展顺利的公司中屡见不鲜，创始人总是在不断施加压力。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: I remember our IPO day. We had this thing. I had to wake up super early. It was a virtual bell ringing, and the second it was over, we had our weekly business review, and there were tough questions being asked. There was not champagne being passed around. I mean, people were in a good mood, but it wasn't like, "Wow, this is so great." It's just like, "Hey, how are we going to serve our customers today?" And I thought that was really emblematic of, "Hey, if we take too deep of a breath and are patting ourselves on the back..." It reminds me of the saying, "Somewhere, someone out there is practicing, and when you meet them, they will beat you." It's the same kind of thing. It's if you take too long to be self-congratulatory, you're going to fall behind the people who are still hungry. So it's important to stay hungry.
turns.zh: 我记得我们上市那天。我们举办了庆典仪式。我不得不早起参加虚拟的敲钟仪式，仪式一结束，我们就开始每周例会，会上提出了许多尖锐的问题。没有人举杯庆祝。当然，人们情绪不错，但没有人欢呼雀跃，只是问："今天我们要如何服务客户？"我觉得这恰恰说明，"如果我们稍作停顿，沾沾自喜..."正如那句谚语所说："在某个地方，总有人在刻苦磨练。当你遇到他们时，他们会击败你。"道理是一样的。如果你停下脚步自我陶醉，就会落后于那些保持饥渴感的人。所以保持饥渴感至关重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. Reminds me, I think it's Bill Gates talking about someone's in a garage building the next Microsoft, and he's always trying to stay ahead of them.
turns.zh: 哇。这让我想起比尔·盖茨谈到某个在车库里打造下一个微软的人的故事，他始终在努力领先对手。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: So true.
turns.zh: 太对了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The other thing this makes me think about is just, it's wild that founders... like Airbnb founders have been at this 15 years. Tony, I'm not exactly sure. We're probably a similar amount of time. It's just like they have to keep that pressure on within the company and also keep themselves motivated and excited and continuing to push. Just such a hard path. There's benefits to being that founder, but it's such a challenging life, too.
turns.zh: 这让我联想到，Airbnb的创始人能坚持15年真是令人惊叹。托尼，我不太确定我们的坚持时间是否相仿。但他们必须在公司内部保持这种压力，同时激励自己、保持激情，不断前进。这条路太艰难了。作为创始人固然有其好处，但这也是一种充满挑战的生活。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: Yeah, I think it can be lonely to be a founder, for sure. I know that Tony's tried to develop a community, for him, of people who are similarly situated from other companies, and that's been helpful. And the real founders that I've come across, that drive, though, is something they can't turn off. They don't have to try to keep it, because there's a handful of traits I've seen that are pretty common. One is a level of obsessiveness. Two is hypercompetitiveness. And I think they're good at manufacturing straw men, even if everyone's saying nice things. It's like Michael Jordan used to take things out of context and make bulletin board material. There's definitely an element of that in the great founders that I've come across. And there's just a raw curiosity. So it's the competitiveness, but the curiosity in learning how things are working, and those all come together to create a drive that just never stops.
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得作为创始人肯定很孤独。我知道托尼曾试图为自己组建一个由其他公司类似处境者组成的社区，这很有帮助。而我接触过的真正的创始人，那种驱动力是无法关闭的。他们无需刻意维持，因为我观察到一些共同的特质。首先是痴迷。其次是超强竞争力。他们善于制造假想敌，即便所有人都说好话，他们也能找到攻击点。就像迈克尔·乔丹会断章取义、拿来当作嘲讽的素材一样。我接触过的优秀创始人身上都有这种特质。还有纯粹的好奇心。因此，竞争力与探索事物运作原理的好奇心交织在一起，共同形成一种永不止息的驱动力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That resonates. Coming back to the DoorDash journey a little bit, I imagine the pandemic was kind of this microcosm of high highs and low lows, where, as an external observer, felt like everyone needed DoorDash immediately, and it was just probably the best thing for your business. On the other hand, I imagine you had to scale like crazy and keep the wheels on the bus through this time. Can you just talk about that part of history for DoorDash?
turns.zh: 说得真在理。再回到DoorDash的发展历程，我想疫情期间既是高光时刻，也是低谷。作为局外人看，当时所有人都迫切需要DoorDash的服务，这对你们的业务来说无疑是绝佳机遇。但另一方面，你们必须疯狂扩张，在那段时期保持业务运转。能否谈谈DoorDash这段历史中的这部分经历？

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: I mean, it was just a wild rollercoaster. We were trying to get ready to go public, first of all, and so there was that overlay. And then, what you saw was our volume dropped right away, like the first or second day of lockdown. And I was like, "Well, this is going out of business because no one wants to order food from restaurants anymore." People didn't know how COVID was transmitted. And so just basically volume dropped out a cliff. And I was like, "Oh, went from a super high. We're getting ready to IPO. Super low. Volume's going to zero." And then, all of a sudden, volume doubled. And that was really exciting for a second, till we realized that our customer support center... I was running support at the time. All the support centers around the world shut down. So you're doubling volume. You have no one to serve it, from a customer support perspective.
turns.zh: 我是说，整个过程简直像过山车一样刺激。首先，我们正准备上市，所以当时面临着诸多挑战。接着，大家看到我们的订单量瞬间暴跌，就像封城最初一两天的情景。我当时就想：“完了，这家公司要倒闭了，因为没人愿意点外卖了。” 那时人们还不清楚新冠病毒的传播方式，所以订单量直线暴跌。我当时特别担心，心想：“从高峰到低谷，订单量几乎归零。”结果突然间订单量翻了一倍。这短暂的兴奋很快被打破，因为全球各地的客服中心都关闭了。订单量翻倍，却没有人能提供服务支持。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: And our infrastructure, we weren't planning to grow that fast. We didn't think there was a chance of two or three exiting in a very short window. And so every Friday night, the app would crash. And if you're running customer support, there's few things you like less than the app going down. Set aside what it means for the customers and for the business. Selfishly, it's just super painful. The irony of it was, is our NPS was going up and that people were just so grateful to have the product, to be able to safely get the things they needed, for people to be able to earn money at times when they really needed it because maybe their job had been shut down, or they weren't allowed to go in. It became a really essential service for folks. And that was really motivating for me, and I think for the team, is to really be able to fulfill the big part of our mission of empowering local economies in a very unique way in a very special time.
turns.zh: 我们的基础设施原本没打算扩展得这么快。我们没想到会在短时间内有两三家公司退出市场。结果每个周五晚上，应用都会崩溃。作为客服人员，最讨厌的就是应用故障。先不说对用户和业务的影响，单就个人而言，这简直让人抓狂。讽刺的是，我们的NPS（净推荐值）反而在上升，用户对产品的感激之情溢于言表。他们能安全获取所需物品，尤其是在因封锁无法工作或被禁止出门的时期，外卖平台成了至关重要的服务。这对我和团队来说，确实是一种激励，让我们能以独特的方式，在特殊时期为赋能地方经济发挥重大作用。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: And the last thing I'll say on the pandemic was, one of my most vivid DoorDash memories was being on a Zoom call, where we were trying to figure out what to do to help restaurants. And again, we were trying to go public. And Tony made a decision, and I admit, I'm on the wrong set of history. I was arguing that this seemed extreme, just to cut commissions by basically 100 million bucks for restaurants, to help them stay in business. And I'm like, "Hold on. We're trying to go public. This is going to completely change the bottom line perspective. No one's asking us to do this."
turns.zh: 关于疫情的最后一点回忆，是我在一次Zoom会议上争论如何帮助餐厅。当时我们正准备上市，托尼做了一个决定。我承认，我当时的立场有失偏颇。我反对削减餐厅佣金1亿美元来帮助他们维持运营，觉得这太极端了。我说：“等等，我们正要上市，这会彻底改变财务状况。没人要求我们这么做。”

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: And Tony says, "Keith, you think too short-term." He's like, "This is the right thing to do." And reminded me of the Ted Lasso quote, which is, "Doing the right thing is never the wrong thing." And talk about how sometimes there's healthy debate. He didn't want to hear any debate on this one. He said, "Just shut it down." And he's like, "Founder-led decision. This is the right thing to do. We're going to cut these commissions." And I woke up the next morning and never been happier to kind of been overruled in a debate before than there. It was just such a meaningful moment for the company, and I was so proud to be a part of the organization.
turns.zh: 托尼说：“基思，你太目光短浅了。”他引用了泰德·拉索的一句话：“做正确的事永远不会是错误的选择。” 他强调有时候需要健康的辩论，但这次他不容置疑：“就这么定了。” 他说：“这是创始人做出的决定，这是正确的选择。我们要削减佣金。” 第二天早上醒来，我从未像那次被否决后这么开心过。这对公司来说是一个意义非凡的时刻，我为能成为这个团队的一员而深感自豪。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything else you took away from that experience of just living through this up and down of pandemic times at DoorDash?
turns.zh: 你从在DoorDash经历的疫情起起落落中还有什么其他收获吗？

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: It actually reminds me of the best advice I got when we were having our first kid. And everyone thinks they're going to give you the insight that's really going to be transformative. But one that stuck with me is, "For better and for worse, everything's temporary. So the highs, you can't get too high. The lows, you can't get too low." That really resonated with me during that period of time, as well as this general idea that you have to try to find opportunities to reach the potential for the business. And decisions sometimes have to be made in very short time horizons, and being able to seize those moments, I think, is really important.
turns.zh: 这实际上让我想起了我们迎来第一个孩子时得到的最佳建议。每个人都觉得自己能给出真正具有变革性的见解，但有一条建议让我铭记于心："无论顺境还是逆境，一切皆为暂时。所以高光时刻别太得意，低谷时刻别太失落。"这句话在那段时期深深触动了我，同时也让我深刻领悟到，必须努力寻找机会，挖掘业务的潜力。而有时，决策必须在极短的时间内做出，而能把握住这些时机，对我而言至关重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I have a few questions about product that I want to get to. But one bigger question about DoorDash is, you've been involved in a lot of the bigger fundraising moments, DoorDash. I think you've worked probably with every major firm out there, raised large dollar amounts for DoorDash. Are there any memories or lessons that you can share from that experience?
turns.zh: 我有几个关于产品的问题想提问。但关于DoorDash的一个更宏观的问题是，你参与了DoorDash的多轮重大融资。我想你几乎与所有主流机构合作过，为DoorDash募集了巨额资金。能否分享一下那些经历中的难忘瞬间或经验教训？

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: We've definitely tried to raise from everyone, been told no many, many times. I mean, raising the Series D was really difficult. Tony and I worked together very closely on that one. And there was a lull in the tech market publicly, and it translated pretty quickly to the private markets. And people didn't believe in either the TAM or the profitability of the business model. And it was difficult. I think one thing that process taught me is after we raised the D, almost every round, or I think every round ended up being led by someone who had passed in a previous round. And that was because we put up numbers we were highly confident we were going to hit.
turns.zh: 我们确实尝试向所有人融资，但被拒绝的次数太多了。比如D轮融资就异常艰难。托尼和我密切合作完成了这轮融资。当时科技市场公众情绪低迷，这一波低迷很快蔓延至私募市场。人们对DoorDash的市场潜力和商业模式的盈利能力都持怀疑态度。整个过程教会了我一个道理：在D轮融资后，几乎每一轮融资都是由之前拒绝过我们的人领投的。这是因为我们提出了极具信心的增长目标。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: I'm an operating partner at a venture firm on the side, and I see that most people put up stretch plans, but they [inaudible 00:46:31]. But that was just not in our DNA. We wanted to make sure that we put forth numbers that we knew were going to hit, and that cost us some dilution upfront in the form of lower valuations, I think. And there's just a trust that builds from that, where when we tell people we're going to do something, that they have conviction that we're going to do it. And I would trade a couple of points of dilution for that level of trust with the right investor base over time.
turns.zh: 我兼职担任一家风投公司的运营合伙人，发现大多数人制定的融资计划都过于乐观，但他们往往（00:46:31处语音中断）。但这并非我们的行事风格。我们坚信必须设定切实可行的增长目标，即便这意味着初期估值被压低。但这样做能赢得投资者的信任，当我们承诺达成目标时，他们会深信不疑。相较于低估值带来的稀释，我更愿意为这种信任与合适的投资者群体长期合作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For founders that are going through fundraising right now, maybe having a hard time, any just advice from that period for founders, yeah, that are having a hard time raising these days?
turns.zh: 对于正在融资却遭遇困难的创业者，有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: It's fortunate because you only need one yes. Right? And you see all the people post the how many rejections they got. Every business that you have heard of has gotten rejected by at least a handful of venture capitalists at one point or another. And so that drive to keep going, if you believe in the business, is critical, absolutely critical. I mean, we were weeks of runway situation and had been told no by everyone, and it was just Tony's drive, really, to keep going. And the way he explains it to me is it's just the difference between a founder and a non-founder. If you're really a founder, you just have to find a way. You have to keep going. There's no question. And I mean, that's the only advice I can give folks, is it only takes one yes. But you got to keep going.
turns.zh: 幸运的是，你只需要一个肯定的答复。不是吗？你看到很多人晒出自己被拒绝的次数。但每个你听说过名字的公司，都曾在某个阶段被多个风投拒绝过。所以，保持前进的动力至关重要。如果你坚信自己的业务，必须找到方法继续前行。托尼曾向我解释，这就是创始人和非创始人的区别。真正的创始人必须想办法继续前进，绝无退路。这是我能给出的唯一建议：只需一个肯定的答复。但你必须坚持下去。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Shifting a little bit to a few product questions. Most listeners to this podcast are product builders, growth people, founders, and so I have a couple questions here. Today you're currently leading the corp dev and BD team, and I imagine you work closely with the product team. And so I'm curious what you've found to be an effective relationship between BD and product and from the experience you've had at DoorDash doing that.
turns.zh: 太棒了。接下来转向几个产品相关的问题。听这个播客的大多数听众都是产品开发者、增长团队成员、创始人，所以我有几个问题想请教。如今你负责公司开发和业务拓展团队，我猜你与产品团队合作得很紧密。我很好奇你发现BD与产品团队之间怎样的合作关系才算高效？从你在DoorDash的经验来看，有哪些经验值得借鉴？

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: Yeah, I joke that our head of product, Rajat Shroff, is actually the head of BD, because he's both interested and good at it. And to do impactful BD, the two really have to go hand-in-glove. So when I think through how to make that relationship work, the first challenge I've confronted, and maybe mistake I made, is trying to figure out what the right cadence is. When do you bring in the product team? Because if you bring them in too early on a deal that really has no chance of getting done, you waste valuable cycles. And our tech talent is our most precious resource, probably, at DoorDash. And so you have to be really mindful about when you bring them in. But if you bring them in too late, it may be a situation where you've given on terms that you really shouldn't have, and that can be really detrimental to the partnership as well.
turns.zh: 是啊，我开玩笑说我们的产品主管拉贾特·施罗夫实际上是BD部门的负责人，因为他对这两方面都感兴趣且擅长于此。要想开展有效的BD工作，两者必须紧密配合。因此，在思考如何建立这种合作关系时，我遇到的第一个挑战——或许也是我犯过的错误——就是试图确定合适的节奏。何时引入产品团队？因为如果在一笔根本没有成功希望的交易中过早引入他们，就会浪费宝贵的资源。在DoorDash，技术人才可能是我们最宝贵的资源，所以引入他们的时机必须谨慎。但如果引入得太晚，可能就会在一些本不该让步的条款上做出让步，这对合作关系也非常不利。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: So I think one thing to do is just give visibility. So without actually bringing them and having a full discussion, like, "Here's the pipeline. If you see things that are super impactful, let us know. If you think things you're not so sure that are going to make a difference, please let us know." That's been really helpful.
turns.zh: 所以我认为一个有效的做法就是提高透明度。即使不实际引入团队并进行全面讨论，也要保持信息共享。比如，“这就是我们的潜在合作伙伴名单。如果你发现有特别有价值的合作机会，请告诉我们。如果你觉得某些合作可能性不大，也请告知我们。”这种做法非常有用。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: Another thing that Rajat's taught me is the importance of building platforms, and whenever you can. So what we used to do is, I'd go out and negotiate a deal. We had a lot of deals around DashPass, which is our subscription product, and I'd ask the product team to go build a bespoke thing for this particular partnership, Chase or whatever partnership we were negotiating at the time. And Rajat said, "Why don't you figure out what the scalable solution is for this? We will build you a product. You won't need to come ask us every time to build something. And then you'll know the parameters in which you can negotiate. You can negotiate a better velocity. We might spend more time on the first version of this, but very little effort for the next. And we'll have a high return on the product hours and the engineering hours spent." And so that was a super valuable insight that I garnered from him, is to try to figure out how to create these type of platforms.
turns.zh: 拉贾特还教会我一个重要的道理：只要有可能，就要搭建平台。我们过去的做法是，我出去谈判交易。围绕我们的订阅产品DashPass，我们有很多合作机会。每次谈判合作伙伴（比如Chase）时，我都会让产品团队为这次合作单独开发定制方案。拉贾特说：“你为什么不先想出一个可扩展的解决方案呢？我们会为你开发产品，这样你就不用每次都来找我们了。这样你就能清楚谈判的边界条件，争取更好的进展速度。我们可能会在第一个版本上花费更多时间，但后续的版本只需很少精力。这样产品团队和工程团队投入的资源就能获得高回报。”这就是我从他那里获得的宝贵见解——要学会搭建这类平台。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Any other lessons of just building an effective BD team within a product company, especially at the scale you're at?
turns.zh: 在产品公司内部建立高效的BD团队，还有哪些经验值得分享？特别是像DoorDash这样规模的公司？

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: A few other things. Number one... This is something else that Rajat taught me. One of our core values is, "Dream big, start small." And he really brought that to the BD product org. And there were some painful times. We invested heavily in a partnership with a hotel chain. We thought we were going to build, "Hey, we're going to make sure that this is the new dine-in experience when you're at a hotel. We can actually replace room service." And asked for a lot of product worked. And it was a total flop. And the realization I had is that we should have gone out and tested this at one hotel with just some hacky operations and seen what the uptick was. And what I would've realized is this particular hotel chain was franchised. So even though corporate thought this was an important thing they were going to prioritize, if the franchisee doesn't care about it, they're not going to give you the visibility, in room or otherwise, to make it work. So we built all this great integration [inaudible 00:51:32] that was totally wasted because the operations weren't right.
turns.zh: 还有几件事要讲。首先……这是拉贾特教给我的另一个道理。我们的核心价值观之一是“梦想远大，脚踏实地”。他真的把这一理念带入了BD产品团队。当然也经历过一些艰难时刻。比如，我们大力投资与一家酒店连锁合作，原以为能打造“酒店内全新用餐体验”，甚至取代客房服务。但最终项目彻底失败了。我意识到，我们本该先在一家酒店进行试点，通过临时性运营验证效果。如果能早点发现，那家连锁酒店是加盟模式。即便总部认为这项业务重要并优先推进，但加盟商若不重视，根本无法获得客房或其他资源支持。于是我们打造的所有整合功能都白费了。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: And I have probably two or three other examples of situations where I learned I should have just gone out and stood out front with a promo code, and handed it out in certain forums, and seen if that changed customer behavior, before going and asking for the product resources. And Rajat correctly was like, "Hey, this is how we have to think about these things going forward." So yeah, definitely building platforms, "Dream big, starts small," use operations to test a thesis around a deal before you actually expend the product resources, I think has been super helpful. And then, the last thing would be to engage early, but not too early, on deal opportunities.
turns.zh: 还有两三个类似案例。比如，我本该先在特定论坛发放优惠码，观察客户行为变化，再申请产品资源支持。但拉贾特一针见血地说：“未来我们必须坚持这种思维方式。”确实，搭建平台时秉持“梦想远大，脚踏实地”的理念，先用运营验证商业假设，再投入产品资源，效果显著。最后要点是尽早介入，但不宜过早。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting how the advice of doing things that don't scale just continues to be useful, even at the scale of a DoorDash. Like you said, you could just stand out there and see if people want room service through DoorDash before building a whole solution.
turns.zh: 有趣的是，即便面对像DoorDash这样的大型平台，保持小规模试错的理念依然适用。比如你提到，可以先在酒店试点，再开发完整解决方案。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: Yeah, early DoorDash, that was a core value. Do things that don't scale. It's as relevant today as it was then.
turns.zh: 是的，DoorDash早期就秉持这一核心价值观。做不易规模化的事。时至今日，这一理念依然意义重大。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Same at Airbnb, is something the founders brought up all the time. And speaking of that, another area that you have a lot of expertise on is legal. So, you led legal for a while at DoorDash. And I was thinking, as thinking about this question, "I wonder what's more difficult, to be head of legal at Airbnb or head of legal at DoorDash," both fraught businesses and ideas. But we'll avoid that question for now. So my question is just legal and product. It's always this interesting relationship, how much legal has say over what happens versus how much product has final decision-making powers. Any lessons there about just how to set up a product and legal relationship within a software business?
turns.zh: Airbnb也是如此，创始人也反复强调这一理念。说到这里，法律事务是你擅长的领域之一。你曾在DoorDash负责法律事务。我在思考这个问题时好奇：“在Airbnb和DoorDash担任法律总监，哪个更具挑战性？”毕竟两家都是高风险、高增长的公司。但先不探讨这个问题。我的问题聚焦于法律与产品关系。这始终是个复杂的平衡，法律部门对项目决策有多大话语权，产品团队又有多大最终决策权？在软件公司中如何构建合理的法律与产品协作机制？

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: Yeah. And both for the product folks that are listening as well as the entrepreneurs who want to be founders, I've had the pleasure of working with two founders who are very product-driven, product-first folks, in Travis and Tony. And I've found that the way they engage on the legal side is with the curiosity I referenced earlier, which is they're both hyper curious, and they will ask questions until they understand the law in the particular area about as well as the lawyers. And then they will apply a first principles product mindset to their understanding of the law, and they will push the lawyers to make sure that they're not being overly conservative, which sometimes they can be.
turns.zh: 是的。对于正在听节目的产品从业者，以及那些渴望成为创始人的创业者来说，我有幸与两位非常以产品为导向、以产品为先的创始人——特拉维斯和托尼——合作过。我发现，他们在法律事务上的参与方式，正如我之前提到的——好奇心驱使。他们都极其好奇，会一直提问，直到他们对特定领域的法律理解得和律师一样透彻。然后，他们会将第一性原理的产品思维应用于对法律的理解，推动律师确保法律条文不过于保守——有时律师确实会过于谨慎。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: And so, when you're on the product team, especially if you're in a consumer-facing business, it may not be as pronounced for SaaS businesses, but if you're in a consumer-facing business, working on a consumer-facing product, you had better have at least a general understanding of what type of regulations are going to apply to your business, and what type of constraints there are, and how to push those constraints. Yeah, and so for me it's just about that level of curiosity and actually engaging in the profession. Right? There's nothing magic about the law. There's a finite number of things that you can learn. And just like all the other functions I've learned, I think you can engage them in a way, till you are proficient and actually really accretive to your business.
turns.zh: 所以，当你身处产品团队时，尤其是如果你的业务面向消费者，SaaS公司可能没那么明显，但如果你从事面向消费者的业务，开发面向消费者的产品，你最好至少对适用于你业务的法规类型、存在的约束条件，以及如何突破这些约束条件有一个大致的了解。是的，对我来说，这就是那种好奇心，以及真正参与到这个专业领域中去。对法律没有什么神奇之处。你能学到的东西是有限的。就像我学过其他职能一样，我认为你可以以某种方式参与其中，直到你精通并真正为你的业务增值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Keith, this has been incredible. I can see why people want to work for you, why they keep giving you more teams to run. I learned a ton. I'm really excited for folks to listen to this and learn from you. Two final questions. Where can folks find you online, or if they want to reach out or learn more, where do you point them? And then, two, how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 基思，这次交流太棒了。我明白为什么人们想为你工作，愿意把更多团队交给你管理。我学到了很多。我真的很期待听众能收听这次对话并从中受益。最后两个问题：听众在哪里可以找到你？如果他们想联系你或了解更多信息，可以去哪里找？然后，第二个问题，听众如何能为你提供帮助？

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: If you want to find me, LinkedIn is the place you can locate me. You can locate me there. I don't do any other social media. It is maybe unusual in this day and age, but that's my preferred medium. And then, as far as being helpful, always looking for referrals for great people. That would be the number one thing. And everyone has an opportunity to use our product. So if you have product feedback, I always welcome that as well.
turns.zh: 如果你想找到我，可以在领英上找到我。我不使用其他社交媒体平台。可能在当今时代这有些不寻常，但这就是我偏好的交流方式。至于提供帮助方面，永远在寻找优秀人才的推荐。这是首要任务。每个人都有机会使用我们的产品。所以如果你有产品反馈，我也非常欢迎。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For folks that maybe want to join DoorDash after hearing this, is there specific roles you're hiring for? Anything you want to share there, folks that might be interested?
turns.zh: 对于可能听完后想加入DoorDash的人，你们目前有特定的职位空缺吗？有任何可以分享的信息吗？

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: Yeah, I mean, select roles definitely on the product and engineering side is a place we're focused right now. But even if there's not a role open today, I like meeting great people. I've found that building relationships over time, even when you're not looking, is impactful.
turns.zh: 是的，我的意思是，产品和工程部门的特定职位是我们目前关注的重点。但即使现在没有职位空缺，我也喜欢结识优秀的人。我发现，即使你不是主动寻找，随着时间推移建立的关系也会产生积极影响。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Keith, thank you so much again for doing this.
turns.zh: 太棒了。基思，再次非常感谢你参与这次交流。

turns.speaker: Keith Yandell
turns.en: Thanks, Lenny.
turns.zh: 谢谢，莱尼。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Thanks for listening. You can find the full episode on YouTube, or head on over to lennyspodcast.com.
turns.zh: 感谢收听。你可以在YouTube上找到完整节目，或访问lennyspodcast.com。
